Alright, I went pretty deep down the rabbit hole on this one.

I started off wanting to build an LED grow light since, it seemed that the absorption spectrum of chlorophyll was limited to 4 separate peaks, two red and two blue. You'll notice that most LED grow lights have pinkish, purplish, red and blue LED emitters. These correspond nicely to the 4 peaks, so you'd think that that'd be all that is needed, and the rest of the energy required to produce all the other components of the light are wasted energy.

I came across this page, and it had a great breakdown of the specific wavelengths I needed:

http://ledgrowlights.blogspot.ca/2006/10/wavelengths-in-led-plant-grow-lights.html

I started online shopping, made lists of 3W, 5W, 10W, 20W and 100W LED emitters. I checked multiple sources, figured out who was exaggerating their light intensity and power rating claims, and found the best prices and the best lumen/watt for the buck. What I determined was that I could put together a grow light for significantly less than buying one.

But I didn't stop there. I kept reading and learned that you can use a green light to illuminate the flowering room during the dark cycle. I learned that green light is also required for the photosynthesis and that there was a difference between absorption spectrum and activation spectrum. This pdf from the University of Colorado Colorado Springs (yes, there are two Colorados in the title) explains it well. Don't believe me, check for yourself:

http://www.uccs.edu/~scastell/ges2050/web/lab_6/what_light_do_plants_need_2012-10-05.pdf

Then I looked at the white light spectrum for cool white, neutral white, and warm white and found that it'd cover what you'd need, pretty well. Dump in a chunk of Deep red LEDs (660 nm) and maybe a cyan LED (480 nm) and you'd be rocking.

So there I had it; I went back to the interweebs and checked different wattage LEDs for different colour temperature LEDs. Great news, it ended up being even cheaper!

Then I took a step back and asked a question that I should have asked at the beginning: Is this better than older, existing technology? Tech that has been used and proven? Was I working on a flawed assumption? Well, hindsight is 20/20 and I didn't know what questions I needed to ask, until I had answered some others, so I'm not going to beat myself up too much for it. You can use my time to make your decision, if you like; but I don't expect anyone to take my word on it. In fact, I'd be thrilled if someone could point out something I missed, but I think I've been pretty thorough. So here's the end analysis:

Ignoring the 480 nm blue LEDs because they're hard to find:

Power Rating Colour Lumens
5 W White (cool) 260
5 W White (neutral) 260
5 W White (warm) 220
5 W Deep Red 120
100 W White (cool) 8000
100 W White (neutral) 8000
100 W White (warm) 8000
100 W Deep Red 4500

For 5 W LEDs:

260 + 260 + 220 + 120 = 860 lm

860 lm / 20 W = 43 lm / W

For 100 W LEDs:

8000 + 8000 + 8000 + 4500 = 28500 lm

28500 lm / 400 W = 71.25 lm / W

HPS lamps usually run about 125 lm / W - 150 lm / W

EDIT: to clarify, I've put my findings in a table. For the LEDs, I've defined a "bulb" as 4 LEDs: 1 cool white, 1 neutral white, 1 warm white and 1 deep red. For the HPS lamp, I've used a 600W HPS Bulb UltraSun by Sunlight Supply; only because it was the first one I found online, that was local.

Type Individual Bulb Power Lumens per "Bulb" Efficiency (lm/W)
LED 20W (4, 5W LEDs) 860 lm 43 lm / W
LED 400W (4, 100 W LEDs) 285000 lm 71.25 lm / W
HPS 600W 81000 lm 135 lm / W

My estimation, the HPS lamps are a clear winner; however, the Green LEDs would still be useful for illumination of the flowering room during the darkness cycle. It may also be useful to use Blue LEDs to augment the flowering cycle.

Phew! That was a lot

TL;DR: LEDs don't beat out HPS lights for growing stuff

Then a lot of the energy from the hsp isn't used by plants. The plants should make more efficient use of plain red light, near their absorption peak.

That was my first thought too, and that was why I had decided design an LED lamp. Blue light is also part of the absorption spectrum for both Chlorophyll A and B. However, if you read that pdf in my post (the one from UCCS) you'll find that yellows and greens are a part of the photosynthesis cycle, they just aren't used by the chlorophyll. There are other factors in the overall photosynthetic cycle that aren't directly related to chlorophyll. This is where the difference between chlorophyll absorption spectrum and phtotsynthetic activation spectrum comes from.
